data.title: Amazon has wall-to-wall free sports coverage on Black Friday
data.description:
Amazon is going bigger with its Black Friday sports marathon, which is now a regular part of its live-event strategy. The lineup includes golf, the NFL, and the NBA. Notably, viewers don't need a subscription or Prime membership to watch any of the sports coverage barrage. The company's goal is to add new Prime Video or Amazon Prime subscribers.

The day starts with the return of The Skins Game, kicking off roughly 15 hours of live programming. The field is Wyndham Clark, Brooks Koepka, and Justin Thomas, who have 31 PGA Tour wins between them, plus rookie Jackson Koivun. Next is Amazon's fourth Black Friday NFL game, Broncos vs. Steelers. The night ends with an NBA doubleheader featuring the defending champion Knicks and the Western Conference champion Spurs.

The football game also comes with some drama after Pittsburgh benched Aaron Rodgers on Tuesday. On Wednesday he criticized coach Mike McCarthy on The Pat McAfee Show, and the Steelers released him. Front Office Sports expects the fallout to bring more eyes to a game between two playoff contenders.

Amazon is facing a tough comparison from a year ago when the Chicago Bears-Philadelphia Eagles game averaged 16.3M viewers, up 21% from 2024 and 70% from the 2023 debut. The 2025 NBA doubleheader averaged 2.09M, up 121%. Last year's marathon was Amazon's biggest single day of live sports ever, so this year's slate has a high bar to clear.

data.title: Gold pares gains as Fed-hike risks linger, eyes first weekly rise in three weeks
data.description:
Key points:
  • Gold pares gains after jumping over 3% earlier in the session
  • Spot silver up nearly 5%, off $38.18/oz lows hit on Wednesday
  • Gold, silver, platinum eye first weekly gain in three weeks

By Sherin Sans

Gold pared gains on Friday as a firm US dollar, rising Treasury yields and a hawkish Federal Reserve outlook kept investors cautious, but bullion remained on track for its first weekly gain in three as bargain buying lifted prices from a 15-month low hit earlier this week.

Spot gold rose 1.6% to $3,622.71 per ounce by 11:05 a.m. ET (1605 GMT), having risen more than 3% earlier in the session. The metal was on track for a weekly gain of nearly 2.5% after posting losses in the previous two weeks.

US gold futures for December delivery gained 2.5% to $3,620.80 per ounce.

"This recent bounce looks more like short-covering/profit taking than a change in trend. The Fed is still hiking, real yields are high and the dollar is near multi-month highs. Until one of those shifts, rallies toward $3,750–3,800 could attract sellers," said Zain Vawda, market analyst at Audacity Capital.

The dollar was still close to its highest level in 22 months, making dollar-priced bullion more expensive for holders of other currencies, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield rose and was off its recent lows.

Gold fell to its lowest level since late August 2025, at $3,426.35 per ounce, on Wednesday after strong US inflation data boosted expectations that the Fed will keep raising interest rates next month and again in early 2027.

"A return to $5,000 is possible, but not in the first half of the year. Gold needs the Fed to stop hiking and the dollar to roll over. If that happens by mid-2027, a recovery toward $4,500 is realistic," Vawda added.

Rising interest rates diminish gold's appeal by boosting returns on competing interest-bearing assets.

Meanwhile, physical gold demand in key Asian hubs improved this week, with jewellery and investment buying picking up in India, while strong retail purchases in China kept local premiums firm.

Spot silver climbed 4.4% to $43.30 per ounce, platinum gained 2% to $1,316.45 per ounce and palladium rose 2% to $890.44.

All three metals were poised for weekly gains.

data.title: Llyoyd Monteiro Takes On VP, Business HR & Talent Acquisition Role At IndiaFirst Life
data.description:
The HR leader will oversee business HR and talent acquisition for the bancassurance business, following a career spanning multiple HR leadership roles

Llyoyd Monteiro has taken on the role of Vice President – Business HR & Talent Acquisition, Bancassurance at IndiaFirst Life.

Monteiro has been associated with IndiaFirst Life for several years, progressing through multiple leadership positions across HR operations, corporate HR and sales HR. Before this appointment, he served as Vice President – Sales HR.

In his new role, he will lead business HR and talent acquisition for the company's bancassurance business, bringing together experience in workforce planning, talent management and HR operations.

During his previous stint as Vice President – Sales HR, Monteiro worked on workforce restructuring initiatives involving more than 1,500 employees. He also contributed to the organisation-wide adoption of HR technology platforms, including Darwinbox and Onex, alongside initiatives in retention analytics, career development and HR governance.

His earlier roles at IndiaFirst Life include Deputy Vice President – Sales HR, Deputy Vice President – Corporate HR & Performance Management Systems, Assistant Vice President – Human Resources, Senior Manager – HR Services and Manager – HR Operations.

Before joining IndiaFirst Life, Monteiro worked with SBI Life Insurance in HR business partnering. His professional experience also includes stints at Tata Consultancy Services, Arthur Andersen and Mustafa Sultan Security Systems.

His areas of expertise include HR business partnering, HRIS integration, global mobility, total rewards, recruitment administration and organisational workforce management.

The appointment adds to IndiaFirst Life's HR leadership capabilities as the insurer continues to strengthen its distribution and bancassurance operations.

data.title: Right Diagnosis, Right Treatment: The Role Of Laboratory Testing In Tackling AMR
data.description:
Laboratory testing and antimicrobial susceptibility analysis can help clinicians identify infections, guide targeted treatment and strengthen efforts to curb antimicrobial resistance (AMR)

It is an instinct many families will recognise. When someone at home develops a fever or persistent cough, the natural response is to reach for what worked before. Yet similar symptoms can have very different causes, and the medicine that was appropriate for one infection may not be right for another. This is where diagnostics can make an important difference.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) occurs when bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites stop responding to antimicrobial medicines. Appropriate use of these medicines is therefore central to preserving their effectiveness. Diagnostics add an important layer of precision by helping clinicians identify the cause of an infection and, where appropriate, determine which antimicrobial is most likely to work.

The scale of the opportunity is significant. In 2023, approximately one in six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections globally was resistant to antibiotics, according to the World Health Organisation. Bacterial AMR was also associated with more than 4.7 million deaths globally in 2021. Without collective action, AMR could contribute to as many as 39 million deaths by 2050.

Resistance rates among pathogens are rising exponentially globally and in India. Carbapenem resistance in Acinetobacter baumannii and Klebsiella pneumoniae has been reported at 70-80 per cent & 40-50 per cent, respectively. Escherichia coli demonstrates fluoroquinolone resistance rates of 70-80 per cent and third-generation cephalosporin resistance of 60-80 per cent, with ESBL production in many Indian healthcare settings, as reported in publications.

Drug- resistant tuberculosis also remains a significant concern, with rifampicin-resistant and multidrug-resistant TB continuing to require rapid molecular diagnosis and drug susceptibility testing for appropriate treatment selection. These trends underscore the importance of diagnostic stewardship, an approach that encourages the right test for the right patient at the right time.

Clinical Cases Highlight Diagnostic Impact

A 65-year-old man with uncontrolled diabetes and a history of severe UTI-related sepsis presented with fever, chills, urinary symptoms and confusion. While empirical antibiotics were initiated, blood and urine cultures identified Klebsiella pneumoniae. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing subsequently established its resistance profile, enabling clinicians to move to a targeted therapy to which the organism was susceptible. Within 72 hours, the fever subsided, and follow-up blood cultures were negative.

Similarly, a 40-year-old man with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis and a history of interrupted treatment underwent molecular and drug-susceptibility testing. The results identified multidrug-resistant TB with resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid, allowing the healthcare team to initiate an appropriate treatment regimen aligned with national guidelines. The patient showed clinical improvement, while timely diagnosis also supported measures to reduce further transmission.

Diagnostics As Part Of The AMR Solution

The role of the laboratory extends well beyond an individual patient. When used appropriately, microbiology, molecular diagnostics and susceptibility testing can help clinicians select more targeted therapies. Over time, the information produced by laboratories also creates a clearer picture of which pathogens are circulating and how susceptibility patterns are changing.

This creates a valuable continuum: better testing can inform better treatment, better treatment can support responsible antimicrobial use, and aggregated laboratory data can strengthen surveillance and public-health decision-making. The World Health Organisation places stronger surveillance systems and laboratory networks, equitable access to diagnostics, and appropriate antimicrobial use among the core objectives of its Global Action Plan on AMR for 2026-2036.

For laboratories, this also brings greater responsibility. The focus cannot simply be on offering more tests. It must be on delivering clinically relevant testing with quality, speed and appropriate interpretation, and ensuring that laboratory insights reach treating physicians in a form that supports decision-making.

Technology is already expanding what is possible. Advances in microbiology, automated identification and susceptibility testing, molecular diagnostics and data analytics can increasingly help clinicians identify pathogens, characterise resistance and make informed treatment decisions. The next step is to make these capabilities part of a broader culture of diagnostic stewardship.

The World AMR Awareness Week 2026 (18th-24th November) theme, "One Health, One Action: Prevent AMR Now," underlines that fighting AMR requires collaboration among clinicians, microbiologists, laboratories, pharmacists, infection-control teams and public-health systems. It also means helping patients understand a simple but important principle: not every infection requires an antibiotic, and when an antimicrobial is needed, the right diagnostic information can help ensure the treatment is appropriate.

Scientific innovation will continue to bring new medicines and diagnostic technologies into healthcare. Alongside that progress sits a bigger responsibility: using the medicines we already have with greater precision and preserving their effectiveness for the patients who will need them tomorrow.

Dr. Rekha Nair

Guest Author

data.title: SAP Weighs At Least 10,000 Job Cuts Amid AI Shift
data.description:
The proposed restructuring could affect at least 9 per cent of the German software company's global workforce, with product, engineering and sales teams facing particular scrutiny

German software major SAP SE is considering cutting at least 10,000 jobs as part of a restructuring exercise to reposition its business around artificial intelligence (AI), according to a Bloomberg report.

The proposed reductions could affect at least 9 per cent of SAP's global workforce of more than 110,000 employees. However, the final number of job cuts has not been decided and could change following discussions with labour representatives, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg.

SAP said it regularly reviews its organisation to align with its business strategy and customer requirements but declined to comment on whether job cuts were being planned.

AI Strategy Drives Restructuring

The reported cuts come as Chief Executive Officer Christian Klein pushes to make AI central to SAP's business and product strategy. The company is reviewing how it develops and sells software, with plans to embed AI capabilities across its applications.

According to Bloomberg, all departments have been asked to identify potential areas for workforce reductions, with product, engineering and sales teams facing particular scrutiny.

The restructuring also follows changes to SAP's executive leadership. Klein has taken over most responsibilities previously handled by product chief Muhammad Alam, whose contract expires in March and will not be renewed. Sales chief Thomas Saueressig has also announced his departure to become chief executive of Ionos Group SE.

Previous Cuts In 2024

The proposed reductions would come less than three years after SAP undertook another major restructuring in 2024, which involved around 10,000 positions and cost approximately 3 billion euros.

That exercise was largely implemented through voluntary departures and employee retraining, while hiring in other business areas kept the company's overall workforce relatively stable.

SAP's latest restructuring discussions also follow comments from Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam at a Morgan Stanley conference last week. He said the company's headcount had increased slightly during the year and added that he would be surprised if the trend did not reverse.

data.title: Vertex Pharma falls after FDA extends review of kidney disease drug
data.description:
By Sriparna Roy

Vertex Pharmaceuticals shares slipped 6% on Friday after the US health regulator delayed its decision on the company's experimental kidney disease drug until next year, pushing back its entry into the increasingly competitive market.

The US Food and Drug Administration late on Wednesday extended its review of povetacicept, developed to treat immunoglobulin A nephropathy — a chronic disease caused by the buildup of immune antibodies in the kidneys. The regulator will now decide on the drug no later than February 28.

The decision marks a setback for the drug that investors view as critical to anchor Vertex's push into kidney disease to diversify beyond cystic fibrosis and pain.

Otsuka's Voyxact and Vera Therapeutics' Trutakna are already approved for the disease. Vera shares jumped 14% in morning trading.

Citi analyst Geoffrey Meacham said the Vertex stock is expected to face near-term pressure as expectations reset but did not see the delay as overall thesis changing.

Vertex's drug targets the immune-system proteins BAFF and APRIL, involved in the production of disease-causing antibodies in autoimmune disorders.

Heading into the decision, there have been investor concerns about the risk of hypogammaglobulinemia, a disorder marked by low blood levels of immunoglobulins that in turn increase the risk of severe infections.

"We assume that the delay is due to FDA taking extra time to scrutinize data in the wake of the recent Citizen's Petition filing by an unnamed party, which requested label monitoring requirements," said Leerink Partners David Risinger.

"Although we cannot predict the FDA label, we are hoping that if blood monitoring is required, it is infrequent and thus does not materially impact commercial prospects," Risinger said.

data.title: Dallas Fed's 12-month Trimmed Mean PCE inflation rate rises in October
data.description:
Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas' 12-month Trimmed Mean PCE inflation rate rose to 2.4% in October from 2.3% in September.

The Trimmed Mean PCE inflation rate is an alternative measure of core inflation in the price index for personal consumption expenditures.

Core PCE inflation rate, which excludes food and energy, was 3.3% over the 12-month period ending in October 26, compared to 3.1% as of September 26.

Headline PCE inflation rate was 3.8% in October, compared to 3.7% in the previous month.

data.title: U.A.E. Set to Lead Gulf Lending Growth as Banks Navigate Credit Risks — Market Talk
data.description: Bank lending is projected to grow 14% in the U.A.E. next year, compared with 9% in Saudi Arabia and 6% in Qatar, Bahrain-based investment bank SICO says. Corporate-focused lenders could initially benefit from greater exposure to floating-rate loans, before retail lenders become more attractive as monetary policy eases. SICO expects two quarter-percentage-point rate increases by the first quarter, with easing beginning in the fourth quarter. Higher borrowing costs could strain asset quality among indebted property and construction companies. However, growing exposure to government-related borrowers could help contain credit losses, while sustained public spending supports borrowing demand. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

data.title: Gulf IPO Activity Slumps Amid Elevated Geopolitical Risks — Market Talk
data.description: Initial public offering activity in the Gulf has slowed sharply this year amid heightened geopolitical uncertainty, Bahrain-based investment bank SICO says. Six IPOs have raised around $1.5 billion so far this year, with most proceeds raised in the first quarter. That compares with 18 IPOs in 2025 and 23 in 2024. Foreign fund outflows from Gulf equities have reached around $2 billion this year, while the S&P GCC Index, which covers stocks across Gulf Cooperation Council markets, has declined 1.2%. SICO expects regional equities to remain volatile as investors seek clarity on geopolitical risks, interest rates and the timing of government projects. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

data.title: Corn, soy basis flat to weaker after autumn harvests
data.description:
Spot basis bids for corn and soybeans were flat to lower at processing plants in the US Midwest on Friday following an influx of supplies from autumn harvests, dealers said.

  • An ethanol plant in Annawan, Illinois, reduced its corn basis by 10 cents for delivery in November. On Wednesday, the plant lowered its bid by 7 cents.

  • A major processor in Decatur, Illinois, lowered its soybean basis by 2 cents per bushel, after a 3-cent drop on Wednesday.

  • In Cincinnati, Ohio, a grain elevator raised its corn and soybean basis bids by 1 cent and 3 cents, respectively.

  • Farmer sales have slowed, with harvesting all but finished, dealers have said.

  • The US Department of Agriculture is slated to issue a weekly update on corn harvesting progress on Monday. The harvest was 94% complete as of November 22.

  • Chicago Board of Trade corn and soybean futures advanced on Friday. Trading was scheduled to end early at 12:05 p.m. CST (1805 GMT) after the markets closed on Thursday for the US Thanksgiving holiday.

data.title: Bitcoin Whales Accumulate $7.4 Billion in BTC, Breaking a Nine-Year Pattern
data.description:
Key takeaways

  • Balances in Bitcoin addresses holding 1,000 to 10,000 BTC rose by 121,117 BTC from September 30 to November 21, worth about $7.4 billion at a reference price of $61,000. Bitcoin fell 29.5% over the same period.
  • This group reduced its holdings in seven of the previous nine fourth quarters. Its 4.29% increase so far in Q4 2026 is the largest fourth-quarter gain since 2020.
  • The group’s unrealized profit margin dropped from 33.9% to 5.7% by November 21, the lowest reading of 2026 in the report.
  • Addresses holding at least 1,000 BTC recorded $2.1 billion in net realized losses through November 21. Exchange inflows from transaction outputs of at least 1,000 BTC also picked up in November.
  • Rising address balances alone cannot establish how much new money entered Bitcoin or whether its price has bottomed.

Bitcoin whales have reversed their usual year-end pattern. Between September 30 and November 21, balances in addresses holding 1,000 to 10,000 BTC rose by 121,117 BTC even though Bitcoin lost 29.5% of its value. At a reference price of $61,000, those additional coins are worth roughly $7.4 billion.

The figures come from CryptoQuant’s November 27 research report, which was supported by crypto lender CoinRabbit. The study excludes exchange and mining-pool addresses from its balance cohorts. Its findings are a snapshot through November 21, not a final tally for the quarter.

The timing matters. NewsBTC recently reported more than $2 billion in US spot Bitcoin ETF outflows. Fund withdrawals and rising whale balances point in different directions, but they measure different things. Neither tells us whether the same investors are moving their money from ETFs into direct Bitcoin ownership.

A broader measure from Maketo’s whale holdings data puts the balance of addresses with at least 1,000 BTC at 7.22 million BTC on November 26, up 54,379 BTC over the preceding 30 days. That group includes exchange and custody addresses, so it provides a separate view of where coins are held rather than an independent check of CryptoQuant’s 121,117 BTC figure.

Bitcoin Whales Reverse Their Year-End Balance Trend

The combined balance of the 1,000 to 10,000 BTC cohort at just under 2.95 million BTC on November 21, up from 2.83 million at the end of September.

Large addresses reduced their balances in seven of the nine preceding fourth quarters. Only 2019 and 2020 escaped that pattern. The 4.29% increase recorded so far this quarter is the largest Q4 gain since 2020, although December could still change the result.

For comparison, the cohort lost nearly 203,000 BTC over Q4 2025. This year’s increase has come during a falling market, rather than a rally.

There is a catch in calling this a $7.4 billion accumulation. The figure values the additional coins at a reference price; it does not measure the dollars spent buying them. Transfers between addresses, including movements across the cohort’s balance thresholds, can change the total without a market purchase.

The increase tells us where Bitcoin is sitting. It does not tell us how much fresh capital is behind it. That distinction matters when liquidity is scarce.

Bitcoin Whales Are Running Out Of Profits To Protect

The 121,117 BTC figure makes for a bullish headline. The number I would pay closer attention to is the remaining profit margin.

Among addresses holding between 1,000 and 10,000 BTC, the unrealized profit margin fell from 33.9% at the end of September to 5.7% on November 21, its lowest reading of 2026 in the report.

The deterioration is even clearer in dollar terms. Combined unrealized profits for addresses holding at least 1,000 BTC stood at about $24 billion on November 21, down from a peak of $294 billion in August 2025.

Across the broader group of addresses holding at least 1,000 BTC, net realized losses reached approximately $2.1 billion in the first 52 days of Q4. The on-chain data suggests that some large holders are already moving coins at a loss rather than waiting for a recovery.

The relevant distinction is between the balance held at a given date and the profit or loss on coins that move. A growing balance does not prevent other coins within the cohort from being spent below their estimated cost basis.

Exchange deposits deserve a closer look, too. Inflows from unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs) of at least 1,000 BTC averaged 5,012 BTC per day in November through the report’s cutoff, compared with 3,239 in October. That is a measure of large coin outputs, not a count of individual whales.

November’s pickup should not obscure the bigger picture: the quarter-to-date average of 3,955 BTC per day remained below the 2019–2025 Q4 average of 4,575 BTC. Large deposits are not proof of sales, and a rise in this metric alone does not establish that selling pressure has intensified.

What Would Confirm A Bitcoin Market Bottom?

The 2018 and 2022 bear markets offer a useful comparison, though not a roadmap for this one.

Balances in the 1,000 to 10,000 BTC cohort declined in both of those fourth quarters. Their average unrealized profit margins were negative, while the group still had a positive margin at the November 21 reading this year.

Today’s accumulation may be a sign that some large holders are willing to retain exposure through the downturn. The address data cannot establish their motives or identify how much of the increase came from new purchases.

I would not call a market bottom on these numbers alone.

A further price decline could wipe out the cohort’s remaining profit cushion. Whether that produces more selling depends on the holders’ liquidity needs and positioning, neither of which can be read directly from address balances.

The next test is whether large-address balances keep rising while net realized losses and large exchange deposits ease. That combination, alongside evidence of renewed spot demand, would make the recovery case more convincing.

For now, the change in year-end positioning is real within CryptoQuant’s measured cohort. Evidence of a durable recovery is still missing.

data.title: Gulf Equities Could Gain 20%-25% Under Favorable Peace Scenario — Market Talk
data.description: Gulf equities could rise 20%-25% over the next year if the Middle East conflict is resolved and oil prices remain elevated, Bahrain-based investment bank SICO says. Higher oil prices would support government spending, benefiting banks, infrastructure companies and energy producers. A peace deal accompanied by lower oil prices could generate returns of around 15%, while a fragile agreement could limit gains to 2%-5%. An escalation disrupting both Hormuz and Red Sea shipping routes could result in losses of 15%-20%, favoring defensive sectors. SICO's base case assumes a lasting resolution in April and oil averaging $80 a barrel in 2027. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

data.title: Canada Posts Budget Deficit in September on Public-Debt Charges — Update
data.description:
By Paul Vieira

OTTAWA--Canada's budget deficit in September was largely unchanged from the same year-ago month, as a solid gain in personal-tax revenue was partly offset by hefty public-debt charges.

Canada's Department of Finance said the budget deficit in September stood at 5.14 billion Canadian dollars (US$3.61 billion), a slight rise from the year-ago C$5.02 billion shortfall. After the first six months of the current fiscal year, Ottawa is running a C$10.50 billion budget deficit, narrower compared with the C$16.09 billion from the same year-ago period.

The September data arrived weeks after the Liberal government's annual budget plan, which contemplates roughly C$140 billion in spending over the next half decade to fortify an economy struggling under the weight of U.S. tariffs. That spending is being partly financed by higher crude-oil prices, as Canada is a net exporter of the commodity.

The recent budget plan anticipates annual deficits of C$50 billion to C$60 billion, or under 2% of gross domestic product, over the next half-decade. The five-year forecast assumes average annual growth of just under 2%, and crude-oil prices averaging C$74 a barrel, or about 20% below current levels.

The public-finance data, available through the department's Fiscal Monitor publication, said total tax revenue in September rose 3.4% from a year ago. A 10% gain in personal-tax receipts was offset by a decline in sales-tax receipts, which officials attributed to the timing of assessments and refunds issued in the month.

Total expenses in September rose 5.1%. That was driven by a 10.4% increase in public-debt charges, due to higher average rates on an increased stock of bonds. Yields have climbed globally, reflecting expectations of higher inflation--fueled by elevated energy prices--and worries about sovereign debt levels.

The Canadian parliament's budget watchdog said in a report this month that a planned increase in nonbudgetary transactions contemplated by Prime Minister Mark Carney means the debt will grow about three times faster than the deficit over the next five years. This might leave federal finances exposed to unexpected rises in rates, the watchdog said.

Write to Paul Vieira at paul.vieira@wsj.com

data.title: Brookfield's Private Assets Seen Trading at Steep Discount Ahead of 2027 Fee Jump — Market Talk
data.description: Investors' in Brookfield's private funds are currently paying roughly 35 cents on the dollar on private business and future performance fees, "offering considerable upside optionality" ahead of a projected 2027 earnings jump, TD Cowen's David Kwan says. Once you strip out Brookfield's stakes in its publicly-traded affiliates, such as Brookfield Asset Management and Brookfield Renewable, the market values its remaining private holdings and expected fund performance fees at about $6 a share, below their $17-a-share book value. Kwan expects the gap to close as Brookfield collects a projected $5 billion in net carry fees over the next three years, noting that realized fees are "poised for an inflection in 2027," alongside steady growth in its insurance arm and a potential major real estate sale. (adriano.marchese@wsj.com)

data.description:
RNS Number : 0491F GCM Resources PLC 27 November 2026  

This announcement contains inside information for the purposes of Article 7 of the Market Abuse Regulation (EU) 596/2014 as it forms part of UK law by virtue of the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 (“MAR”) and is disclosed in accordance with the Company’s obligations under Article 17 of MAR.

27 November 2026

GCM Resources plc

("GCM" or the "Company")

Suspension of Chief Executive Officer

Changes in Leadership Responsibilities

and

Receipt of Requisition Letter

GCM Resources plc (LON: GCM), an AIM quoted mining and energy company, announces that Datuk Michael Tang, has been suspended from his role as Chief Executive Officer and all other functions within the business with immediate effect.

Datuk Michael Tang will remain suspended, pending the outcome of an investigation into matters relating to his professional conduct. This includes, but is not limited to, an understanding of the circumstances that resulted in him becoming indirectly interested in 43,328,253 ordinary shares of 1 pence each in the share capital of the Company (“Ordinary Shares”), as announced by the Company on 26 November 2026.

The Company proposes to undertake a full investigation, supported by its professional advisers.

Change in leadership responsibilities

Whilst this process is ongoing, at the request of the other Board members, Gary Lye, the Company's Chief Operating Officer, has agreed to temporarily assume the role and responsibilities of Chief Executive Officer, without joining the Board, while the investigation is ongoing.

GCM remains focused on progressing the Phulbari Coal and Power Project, including its ongoing engagement with the Government of Bangladesh and its strategic development partners. The Company will make further updates to shareholders in due course.

Requisition Letter

The Company further announces that it has received a letter dated 27 November 2026 (the "Letter") from Michael Tang on behalf of Polo Investments Limited (the “Requisitioner”) seeking, as holder of not less than 5 per cent. of the paid-up share capital of the Company, to requisition a general meeting (the "GM") of the Company's shareholders under section 303 of the Companies Act 2006, as amended (the "Act").

The Letter includes, amongst other matters, a resolution to remove Charlie Green as a director of the Company with immediate effect as well as resolutions to appoint three additional directors to the Board.

Polo Investments Limited (“Polo Investments”) is the holder of 43,328,003 Ordinary Shares, representing approximately 11.50% of the Company’s issued share capital. As noted in the Company’s announcement on 26 November 2026, the Company was informed that Mettiz Capital Limited (“Mettiz Capital”) is the sole shareholder of Polo Investments. Mettiz Capital is owned and controlled by Datuk Michael Tang.

The Company is taking legal advice as to the validity of the Requisitioners’ Letter, including taking into account the circumstances surrounding Datuk Michael Tang’s obtaining his indirect interest in the Company, and a further announcement will be made in due course.

Under the AIM Rules for Companies and AIM Rules for Nominated Advisers, the Company's Nominated Adviser is required to undertake a director due diligence process to satisfy itself as to board composition, independence, suitability and the efficacy of the board as a whole in relation to any potential board changes for the purposes of the AIM Rules for Nominated Advisers, with a view to determining that the Company is suitable to be a Company with shares admitted to trading on AIM.

About GCM Resources

GCM Resources plc (LON: GCM), the AIM resource exploration and development, has identified a high-quality coal resource of 572 million tonnes (JORC 2004 compliant) at the Phulbari Coal and Power Project (the "Project") in north-west Bangladesh.

Utilising the latest highly energy efficient power generating technology the Phulbari coal mine can support some 6,600MW. GCM requires approval from the Government of Bangladesh in order to develop the Project. The Company has a strategy of linking the Company's mine proposal to supplying coal to the Government of Bangladesh’s existing and in the pipeline coal-fired power plants and / or power plants developed development partners. Together with credible, internationally recognised strategic development partners, GCM aims to deliver a practical power solution to provide the cheapest coal-fired electricity in the country, in a manner amenable to the Government of Bangladesh.
